extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and research-integrity advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the integrity and quality of journal peer-review processes (especially for conference proceedings and guest-edited issues) and identifying signals of paper-mill or fraudulent publication activity. Useful for publishers, editors, and integrity investigators deciding on retraction/withdrawal or editorial-policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review must meet journal's high standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer-review process must meet the 'high standards expected' by the journal; failure to do so can warrant withdrawal/retraction of papers or entire proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in the representative notice: 'the peer-review process was confirmed to fall beneath the high standards expected by Materials Today: Proceedings.' When an investigation shows review fell below standards, the publisher withdrew the entire Proceedings 'in order to correct the scholarly record.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Papers should be on-topic for the venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Published papers should be relevant to the stated scope of the conference/journal; numerous 'off-topic papers' are a red flag for compromised review or paper mills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigation found 'at least 1,500 off-topic papers' in the title, which supported action against the proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts should not contain 'tortured phrases' or machine-paraphrase artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract language should read as coherent scholarly prose; 'tortured phrases' may indicate translation/paraphrasing software or automated generation and are a sign of suspect submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports many abstracts containing 'tortured phrases' that may have been written by translation or paraphrasing software; automated detection of such patterns was recommended for large-scale screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence of authorship/position-for-sale or sold authorship links
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles or author positions advertised for sale (e.g., online listings selling authorship slots) are evidence of unethical practices and undermine publication legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators found 'a few with titles that had been previously advertised with author positions for sale online' — such findings support retraction or withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conferences must be verifiable and actually held
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference organizaton must be genuine and verifiable; suspicion that a conference 'may have never taken place (even virtually)' is grounds for questioning the legitimacy of its published proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsevier investigators suspected some conferences never occurred; verifying event existence and program/chair legitimacy is part of validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should avoid over-reliance on conference organisers' integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial policy should not depend solely on trusting conference organizers; publishers need processes to validate and audit conferences and guest editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsevier noted plans for 'major changes to the structure and editorial process for this journal to avoid over-reliance on the integrity of conference organisers.' The journal had been 'following detailed process for validating conferences and conferences organisers for several years' but still found detection challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated, large-scale screening for suspicious language patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use automated tools to scan many papers for linguistic or stylistic fingerprints of paper mills or machine generation (e.g., repetitive odd phrasing, unnatural collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsevier requested: 'If you have the capability to automatically check large numbers of papers for suspicious language patterns, that would be incredibly helpful for this investigation.' Automated checks are recommended before or alongside manual review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual individual article checks when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform manual, article-level checks of content as part of investigations into suspect proceedings or when automated screening raises flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsevier stated they 'have not started manual checking the content of papers yet on an individual article level' but implied this is part of a complete investigation; manual review can confirm findings from automated scans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for wholesale copying of legitimate conference websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether conference organizers have copied content from legitimate conference websites to fabricate legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes 'conference organizers regularly wholesale copy the content of legitimate conference websites, to create the appearance of a legitimate conference.' Verifying unique website content and provenance is a practical check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conference proceedings and guest-edited issues as higher-risk for paper mills
rubrics_metrics.description: Be especially vigilant with conference proceedings and guest-edited issues, which are 'particularly vulnerable to paper mills' and have been the source of large batches of retractions/withdrawals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: IOP Publishing retracted 850 related papers; ACM retracted over 300. Publishers should apply stronger validation and oversight to these formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and apply appropriate labels (withdrawal vs retraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on correct publication-status taxonomy (withdrawal vs retraction) and apply it consistently to correct the scholarly record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter noted Elsevier lists these depublications as 'Withdrawals' rather than 'Retractions.' Publishers should be transparent and consistent about the chosen designation and its implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize guest editors for conflicts and excessive self-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate guest editors who publish numerous papers in their own special issues or who disproportionately include work from their network/institution, as this may indicate abuse of editorial privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged Elsevier to investigate special issues where editors or their colleagues authored many papers; monitoring editor publication patterns and conflicts of interest is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize quality over quantity in conference organization and editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference organizers and editors should prioritize the quality of submissions and rigorous review rather than maximizing the number of accepted papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments stated 'The conference organizers should not go for quantity but rather quality' to avoid extra work and embarrassment; editorial policies should reflect that value.
